FERAL WISDOMFinding the pearls of wisdom in all the yapping on the feral druid discord
#agility-is-threat-neutral#hit-doesnt-matter
Tanager

I read everything in the feral discord literally when I started tanking, and found some of the slogans (e.g. "agility is threat neutral") pretty confusing as they aren't literally true. However, I've learned there is a lot of wisdom baked down into these slogans, and I've tried to pull out the lessons here.

Some of what came out is new, as far as I know, such as the plots that count the proportion of pulls in which a dps pulls aggro off a feral. These help show the impact of hit, expertise, sappers, and trinkets at the start of the fight.

agility is a mitigation stat with minor threat benefit

  • agility has a small positive effect on threat, both averaged over the fight and on the pull

    +0.21 to +0.31 TPS per point of agilitypositive for every gear set and damage profile, negative only at 80% dodge (above P5 BiS)
    • gear level
    • damage profile
    • not real gear

    Threat (measured in threat per second, TPS) per point of agility, simmed on Morogrim Tidewalker (a level 73 raid boss), falls as avoidance rises, from pre-raid gear down to P5, and only turns negative at 80% dodge (above P5 BiS), in the grey rows where dodge rating is added directly rather than from gear. The middle rows swap the boss's damage profile instead: how hard and how often it swings, which matters because being hit is where most of a bear's rage comes from. Each point is an average over eight independent runs of the sim, and the short dashes either side of it span one standard error of that average, so a point whose dashes stay clear of zero is positive by more than the run-to-run noise.

    Details

    Agility adds dodge, armor, and crit. Dodge and armor both reduce rage (by avoiding being hit or being hit less hard), and crit increases rage, so agility has a mixed effect. But, averaged over a fight, on net agility does increase threat, albeit by a small amount.

    In the grey rows agility does eventually turn negative. So “agility is threat neutral” is only true at very high levels of avoidance.

    • A dead tank generates no threat, so deaths drag a row's average down. The pre-raid row still dies in about 13% of fights even with healing raised to 8,000 HPS (healing per second; the sim's default is 2,200). The hardest-hitting damage profile dies in 5% of fights, and every other row is at 3% or less.
    • run on 2026-08-16, 2026-08-17, on wowsims TBC at 540d9df8a6, built and run natively
    • Each point comes from a paired sim, with and without +20 agility, averaged over 8 independent seeds of 12,500 iterations each. The short dashes on either side of a point span one standard error of that average, so a point whose dashes stay clear of zero is positive by more than the seed-to-seed noise. The two halves of each row's label link the two runs. A link reruns one seed at the same iteration count, so the last digit will vary. Note: The sim website prints a ± of its own beside TPS, which is typically much larger than the ±'s reported here. That value is the pull-to-pull spread. The number here is an average over a hundred thousand pulls, and its ± is how far that average would move if the whole measurement ran again, which is much narrower. Here we care about the variability in the average because we are trying to rank these choices by their effect in aggregate over many pulls.

    However, looking at threat averaged over a whole fight does not tell the full story. Typically the first few seconds are the most important; with a good rotation (and no threat resets), a feral should be able to hold threat easily in the long run. So here we simulate a pull three thousand times and count how often a P2 best-in-slot fury warrior passes the tank.

    • the tank loses threat
    • the tank keeps threat

    In the figure, each line shows the fury warrior's threat as a share of the tank's in one pull. At 110% the warrior pulls aggro, so a line that touches the dashed line is a pull the tank lost; these are colored orange. Most of the losses happen in the first few seconds, and half of them by 2.4 seconds. Using this technique, we can estimate what proportion of pulls the tank loses in a given scenario. Below, we plot the difference in this percentage between a scenario with +200 agility added, and one without (this method is a bit noisy, so we use a lot of agility to see its impact).

    Details
    • run on 2026-08-16, on wowsims TBC at 540d9df8a6, built and run natively
    • each configuration uses 3,000 single-iteration debug runs of the same two-player request (seed k is k×1,000,003); the fury runs in from 12 yards, arriving at 0.93s, and never throttles its damage, so these pull rates are higher than a real raid would see. The panel draws 300 of its 3,000 pulls, taken evenly from the pulls where the tank loses threat and evenly from the rest so that the drawn lines carry the run's own share of losses, and shows the first 20 seconds of each; the percentage on the panel is all 3,000 pulls over the whole 60 seconds. The tank and the fury are two players in one simulation, each in its own party, so both of their threat totals come out of that run's event log, and the fury pulls the boss at the first moment its threat passes 110% of the tank's. The fury's gear, talents and rotation are the P2 fury warrior presets that ship with the simulator, with Blessing of Salvation on, and its party keeps a full set of buffs in every configuration. How often it pulls depends a lot on how both players behave, so these percentages aren't a prediction of what a particular raid would see. Each comparison changes one thing and leaves the behaviour alone, so the difference between two configurations carries over even where the percentages themselves don't.
    • gear level
    • damage profile
    • not real gear

    In each case, we see adding 200 agility reduces the chance the warrior pulls aggro, by between 1.8 percentage points and 5.2 percentage points, so agility helps threat on the pull.

    Details

    The pull-based measurement agrees with the TPS measurement except at the far end. Past any gear, at 80% dodge, a point of agility adds roughly nothing to threat over a fight, because by then the rage its dodge costs has caught up with the crit it adds. On the pull it still helps, probably because the rage takes a while to go missing and the crit doesn't: half of these pulls are lost inside two and a half seconds, before a dodge that saved the tank a hit has cost it a Maul.

    Note that there is nothing special about agility here (unlike hit and expertise, as we will see later): attack power that adds the same amount of threat lowers the pull rate by about as much.

    • This is all simulated in wowsims (tbc-new) rather than measured in game. The sim has its own model of how a bear generates rage, which may be imperfect. The exact version we ran is linked below.
    • The warrior wears its P2 set and stands in its own group with a full set of buffs, both the same in every row, so the tank is the only thing that changes.
    • run on 2026-08-16, 2026-08-17, on wowsims TBC at 540d9df8a6, built and run natively
    • each configuration uses 3,000 single-iteration debug runs of the same two-player request (seed k is k×1,000,003); the fury runs in from 12 yards, arriving at 0.93s, and never throttles its damage, so these pull rates are higher than a real raid would see. The tank and the fury are two players in one simulation, each in its own party, so both of their threat totals come out of that run's event log, and the fury pulls the boss at the first moment its threat passes 110% of the tank's. The fury's gear, talents and rotation are the P2 fury warrior presets that ship with the simulator, with Blessing of Salvation on, and its party keeps a full set of buffs in every configuration. How often it pulls depends a lot on how both players behave, so these percentages aren't a prediction of what a particular raid would see. Each comparison changes one thing and leaves the behaviour alone, so the difference between two configurations carries over even where the percentages themselves don't. Each row is a pair of runs at the same 3,000 seeds, the configuration as it is and the same configuration with 200 agility added, and the point is the difference between them counted pull by pull. The chunk is 200 rather than the +20 the chart above probes with, because one point of agility changes the pull rate by about a fifth of a percentage point, which 3,000 pulls cannot see, so these rows say what a large amount of agility does rather than what the next point is worth.

  • agility is a poor threat stat

    +4.11 TPS for +15 agility, +36.5 for 2% threat, +156 for an enhance shaman
    • a gear choice
    • not gear

    The chart compares how much threat each option adds, and agility is at the bottom. The second group of bars shows non-gear choices, which have a big impact. Each party buff adds more threat than the best enchant, and pressing mangle on cooldown (about 10 casts per minute, or cpm) rather than 6 cpm is worth roughly four enchants.

    Details

    In the gear group the 2% threat enchant adds the most per glove slot (while providing no mitigation or damage at all), followed by expertise, hit below the cap, and strength. Agility is the smallest of them: strength adds about two and a quarter times as much threat per point. The gaps between them are fairly wide.

    This gear set is already at the hit cap, where more hit is worth exactly +0.00, so the hit bar shows the last fifteen rating before the cap instead.

    In the party group, a warrior's Battle Shout, an enhancement shaman's totems and Unleashed Rage, and a BM hunter's Ferocious Inspiration each add more threat than the best enchant (the shaman roughly four times as much). Dropping from mangle on cooldown (about ten casts a minute) to eight a minute costs about two enchants' worth of threat, and dropping to six a minute costs about four.

    • This is all one gear set on one boss, varying one thing at a time, so the ordering could plausibly shuffle a bit on a different gear set or a different fight.
    • The party bars are measured by removing each buff from a fully-buffed group, so each is measured with all the others present. Added one at a time to a tank with no group buffs they are worth more.
    • The capped mangle rows limit the sim to a fixed number of casts per minute, which spreads the skipped casts evenly across the fight.
    • Other threat improvements can come from weapon choice (can vary by a lot of AP) and misdirects.
    • run on 2026-08-17, on wowsims TBC at 540d9df8a6, built and run natively
    • Each bar shows a paired difference over 8 independent seeds of 12,500 iterations, at 8,000 HPS so the tank mostly survives. The second group is measured by removal: the baseline raid has each of these, and the bar is what its absence costs.

    Next, like before, we will measure threat a different way: by seeing what proportion of pulls a BiS fury warrior pulls aggro off a BiS feral tank. Each bar below shows the change in percentage points of how often the warrior pulls aggro, over three thousand simulated pulls.

    • a gear choice
    • not gear

    Here, negative is good (the change is reducing the fraction of pulls in which the warrior pulls aggro), with more negative being better. For example, the enhance shaman bar at −7.5 means the tank kept about seven pulls in a hundred that it had been losing. Mangling is the biggest of them by a long way: a tank that never presses it loses the boss in 70.0% of pulls against 20.5% for one pressing it on cooldown. Losing every one of the party buffs at once, rather than one at a time, takes that 20.5% to 47.0%. And there's no visible benefit from +15 agility here (+0.1 points, with an uncertainty of 0.2), though further down the chart the Badge of Tenacity, 150 agility pressed with the pull, does show a small one (−1.6 points). So agility does seem to have a minor benefit on the pull, just one too small to see at 15 points.

    Details

    Two things sit differently here than they do on the fight average. Expertise and hit come out ahead of the 2% threat enchant, the reverse of the order above, likely because landing the opening mangle and first hits are very important.

    The last group shows on-use trinkets and sappers which tend to have very little impact on average over the whole fight, but have a big impact on holding threat. Moving the super sapper from the sim's default schedule to the pull itself is worth about as much as mangling on cooldown rather than three times a minute.

    • The party bars are measured by removal, one buff at a time from a fully-buffed group. On this axis that understates them by more than it does on the fight average, because a tank with none of the others has many more pulls left for the one buff to rescue.
    • The sapper and trinket bars assume the item is off cooldown at the pull, and the trinket bars swap the second trinket slot, so each carries its item's equipped stats as well as the button.
    • run on 2026-08-17, on wowsims TBC at 540d9df8a6, built and run natively
    • each configuration uses 3,000 single-iteration debug runs of the same two-player request (seed k is k×1,000,003); the fury runs in from 12 yards, arriving at 0.93s, and never throttles its damage, so these pull rates are higher than a real raid would see. The tank and the fury are two players in one simulation, each in its own party, so both of their threat totals come out of that run's event log, and the fury pulls the boss at the first moment its threat passes 110% of the tank's. The fury's gear, talents and rotation are the P2 fury warrior presets that ship with the simulator, with Blessing of Salvation on, and its party keeps a full set of buffs in every configuration. How often it pulls depends a lot on how both players behave, so these percentages aren't a prediction of what a particular raid would see. Each comparison changes one thing and leaves the behaviour alone, so the difference between two configurations carries over even where the percentages themselves don't. Each bar is a pair of runs at the same seeds, with and without the choice, counted pull by pull, and the number beside it carries one standard error. Every row is measured with everything else in place, and the warrior's own group is untouched throughout, so the party rows price what a buff does for the tank.

  • most of agility's value is in mitigation

    +15 agility: −2.4% damage taken (dtps), +0.2% threat (tps)fifteen agility measured both ways, then split into dodge, armor and crit

    Agility gives dodge, crit, and armor.

    15 agilitydodgearmorcrit
    no buffs/talents+1.02%+30+0.60%
    with kings and talents+1.16%+34+0.68%

    We can sim each of those on its own, against the same baseline configuration, and see what each one does to damage taken and threat.

    15 agility, one part at a timedodgearmorcrittogether
    damage taken (dtps)−2.33%−0.07%+0.00%−2.38%
    threat (tps)−0.17%+0.00%+0.39%+0.22%

    So most of agility's value is in mitigation, and nearly all of that is the dodge.

    Details

    Dire Bear Form multiplies armor from gear by 5.5 but doesn't multiply the armor agility gives at all. A point of agility is worth about 1.46 dodge rating and almost exactly 1 crit rating.

    • This is measured with healing raised to 8,000 HPS. At the sim's default 2,200 the tank dies in two pulls out of three, and a dead tank generates no threat, so those numbers would mostly be measuring survival.
    • Damage taken here is averaged over the whole pull.
    • run on 2026-08-15, on wowsims TBC at 540d9df8a6, built and run natively
    • each bar shows the mean of 8 independent 12,500-iteration seeds, and the link reruns one of them

hit is a good threat stat, but non-gear choices matter more

  • Hit is the best threat stat after expertise, both during bad openers and over the fight.

    expertise 9.6 AP per rating, hit 4.4; during bad openers, 13.9 and 7.5seven stats measured two ways, over a fight and during bad openers
    attack power per point of…fight averagebad opener (p10, first 10s)
    expertise below the soft cap, per rating / baseline9.64 ± 0.0313.87 ± 0.14
    expertise above the soft cap, per rating / baseline4.17 ± 0.038.56 ± 0.10
    hit, per rating / baseline4.43 ± 0.047.48 ± 0.11
    strength, per point / baseline2.25 ± 0.012.29 ± 0.02
    crit, per rating / baseline1.78 ± 0.012.16 ± 0.06
    haste, per rating / baseline1.77 ± 0.041.14 ± 0.06
    agility, per point / baseline0.93 ± 0.050.88 ± 0.06
    armor penetration, per point / baseline0.36 ± 0.000.35 ± 0.00

    Here we tabulate how much threat one point of each stat adds, divided by how much threat a point of attack power adds, so the numbers read as attack-power equivalents (a stat at 2.0 adds twice as much threat per point as attack power does). Hit comes out at 4.43 over the fight average and 7.48 during bad openers, behind expertise in both columns, and the next stat down is strength at 2.25 and 2.29. Each ± is the seed-to-seed standard error over the eight runs, so two rows further apart than that differ by more than the noise between runs. Expertise and hit gain roughly half again their value in bad openers and crit gains about a fifth, while haste loses about a third of its; strength, agility and armor penetration barely move.

    Details

    The sims use a P2 best-in-slot feral tank on Morogrim Tidewalker, a level 73 raid boss. Each value comes from a pair of sims, with and without a chunk of the stat, averaged over eight independent seeds of 12,500 iterations. The middle column measures average TPS over a three-minute fight, with healing set high enough that deaths don't cut the threat short. And the right column pins the fight to exactly ten seconds and shows the 10th percentile of the per-pull TPS distribution, as a proxy for pulls where the opener went badly.

    Often, an opener goes badly when the first swings miss or get dodged or parried, and hit and expertise are the two stats that directly help with that, which explains why their value grows in bad pulls relative to the average pull. Each point of expertise removes both dodge and parry from the attack table; the soft cap is when all the dodge has been removed, at which point additional expertise only helps by reducing the chance of parries.

    • run on 2026-08-15, on wowsims TBC at 540d9df8a6, built and run natively
    • each slope comes from a paired sim, with and without a chunk of the stat, over 8 independent seeds of 12,500 iterations. The bad opener column pools the seeds' histograms and interpolates the 10th percentile inside its 10-TPS wide bins. Each ± is the seed-to-seed standard error of that row's own slope, so two rows separated by more than their errors differ by more than the noise between seeds. The attack-power slope itself, the number every row is divided by, is only known to 0.4% over the fight and 0.6% in the opener. That uncertainty is left out of the ± because it moves every row in a column together, so it cannot change how two rows compare. Note: The sim website prints a ± of its own beside TPS, which is typically much larger than the ±'s reported here. That value is the pull-to-pull spread. The number here is an average over a hundred thousand pulls, and its ± is how far that average would move if the whole measurement ran again, which is much narrower. Here we care about the variability in the average because we are trying to rank these choices by their effect in aggregate over many pulls.

  • Expertise and hit are more valuable on the pull than the threat they add over a fight indicates.

    the tank loses threat in 20.5% vs 24.5% of pulls, same average threatthe hit cap traded for attack power, average threat held equal
    • the tank loses threat
    • the tank keeps threat

    This was already shown to some extent in the table above, in the column with the 10th percentile of the threat over the first 10s of the fight. The panels here measure the pull a second way, by racing the tank against a P2 best-in-slot fury warrior with Blessing of Salvation on the same boss, and counting a pull as lost when the warrior's threat reaches 110% of the tank's. Half the losses happen inside 2.4 seconds, so this gives a more nuanced picture than the ten-second average, at the cost of precision: three thousand pulls per configuration rather than a hundred thousand, which puts about ±0.7 percentage points on each of the numbers below.

    In this scenario, we put the warrior in its own group with the best four party members it could have (a feral druid, an enhancement shaman, and two beast-mastery hunters), which is the same in every configuration, so the only thing that changes between them is the tank. Each line is a single pull, with both characters simulated together from that pull's own random seed, and shows the warrior's threat as a share of the tank's, so a line that touches the dashed line at 110% is a pull where the warrior pulls aggro, assuming they never check a threat meter. The percentages count all three thousand pulls, and each panel draws an even sample of 300 of them. The left panel shows the pulls with the feral wearing the hit-capped P2 balanced best-in-slot gear set, and on the right the same set except with 95 hit rating swapped for 456 attack power, which keeps the same average threat over the fight.

    As the panels show, the tank loses the boss in 20.5% of pulls carrying the hit and 24.5% carrying the attack power instead, a gap of 4.0 ± 0.7 points, so while the average threat over the fight is the same, the hit set reduces the chances the warrior pulls aggro.

    Details
    • The fury's 12 yards are a choice, and every percentage on this page rests on it: starting it closer raises them all, starting it farther lowers them all. The gaps between configurations are what survives that choice.
    • The two measures agree on which stats gain and disagree on by how much. Party buffs are worth about 1,130 attack-power equivalents in the ten-second measure and 26.5 pull points here, while the whole hit cap is worth about 700 and 4.0, so the ten-second number doesn't convert to pulls at a fixed rate.
    • run on 2026-08-17, on wowsims TBC at 540d9df8a6, built and run natively
    • each configuration uses 3,000 single-iteration debug runs of the same two-player request (seed k is k×1,000,003); the fury runs in from 12 yards, arriving at 0.93s, and never throttles its damage, so these pull rates are higher than a real raid would see. Each panel draws 300 of its 3,000 pulls, taken evenly from the pulls where the tank loses threat and evenly from the rest so that the drawn lines carry the run's own share of losses, and shows the first 20 seconds of each; the percentage on the panel is all 3,000 pulls over the whole 60 seconds. The panels share their seeds rather than their pulls: one seed gives two runs the same random stream, and the change between the panels sends them apart at the first roll it affects. The tank and the fury are two players in one simulation, each in its own party, so both of their threat totals come out of that run's event log, and the fury pulls the boss at the first moment its threat passes 110% of the tank's. The fury's gear, talents and rotation are the P2 fury warrior presets that ship with the simulator, with Blessing of Salvation on, and its party keeps a full set of buffs in every configuration. How often it pulls depends a lot on how both players behave, so these percentages aren't a prediction of what a particular raid would see. Each comparison changes one thing and leaves the behaviour alone, so the difference between two configurations carries over even where the percentages themselves don't. The 456 AP is bisected so the two panels' 180-second average threat matches to within a fraction of a TPS; with the mean held level, the pull gap can only come from the shape of the opener. That is more than the attack-power equivalent the table below puts on the hit cap, which prices hit at the cap, where nothing is lost to missing. The compensated set misses 6% of its swings, so each point of attack power it carries is worth about 6% less, and it takes more of them to hold the average level.

    Expertise works the same way until its hard cap. Each of the four panels below shows one configuration at one level of expertise, with compensating attack power so that all four have the same average threat over the full fight.

    • the tank loses threat
    • the tank keeps threat
    Details

    The tank loses the boss in 24.4% of pulls with no expertise and 575 attack power in its place, 20.5% wearing the 63 rating the baseline carries, 16.4% at 103 rating, where the boss can no longer dodge, and 9.8% at 221 rating, where dodge and parry are both gone and the gap between expertise and hit mostly closes.

    • run on 2026-08-17, on wowsims TBC at 540d9df8a6, built and run natively
    • each configuration uses 3,000 single-iteration debug runs of the same two-player request (seed k is k×1,000,003); the fury runs in from 12 yards, arriving at 0.93s, and never throttles its damage, so these pull rates are higher than a real raid would see. Each panel draws 300 of its 3,000 pulls, taken evenly from the pulls where the tank loses threat and evenly from the rest so that the drawn lines carry the run's own share of losses, and shows the first 20 seconds of each; the percentage on the panel is all 3,000 pulls over the whole 60 seconds. The panels share their seeds rather than their pulls: one seed gives two runs the same random stream, and the change between the panels sends them apart at the first roll it affects. The tank and the fury are two players in one simulation, each in its own party, so both of their threat totals come out of that run's event log, and the fury pulls the boss at the first moment its threat passes 110% of the tank's. The fury's gear, talents and rotation are the P2 fury warrior presets that ship with the simulator, with Blessing of Salvation on, and its party keeps a full set of buffs in every configuration. How often it pulls depends a lot on how both players behave, so these percentages aren't a prediction of what a particular raid would see. Each comparison changes one thing and leaves the behaviour alone, so the difference between two configurations carries over even where the percentages themselves don't. Every rung holds the 180-second average threat equal: the expertise panels debit the attack power their expertise rating is worth, bisected to within a fraction of a TPS, so the ladder isolates what avoidance-removal does to pulls. 221 expertise rating is far above the 63 the baseline wears; the panel shows the asymptote.

    These scenarios artificially boost or reduce stats (adding expertise or hit or AP without changing gear). One realistic gear swap to consider for pull variance is Romulo's Poison Vial with its 35 hit rating versus the Abacus of Violent Odds with its 260 haste on use for ten seconds. Consistent with the conventional wisdom, Abacus wins here: used on the pull, the tank loses the boss in 16.0% of pulls versus 20.5% with the vial, despite giving up the hit.

The tank and the fury are two players in one simulation, each in its own party, so both of their threat totals come out of that run's event log, and the fury pulls the boss at the first moment its threat passes 110% of the tank's. The fury's gear, talents and rotation are the P2 fury warrior presets that ship with the simulator, with Blessing of Salvation on, and its party keeps a full set of buffs in every configuration. How often it pulls depends a lot on how both players behave, so these percentages aren't a prediction of what a particular raid would see. Each comparison changes one thing and leaves the behaviour alone, so the difference between two configurations carries over even where the percentages themselves don't.

  • Non-gear choices probably have a bigger effect on threat than gear choices.

    full party buffs are worth ~1,210 AP of gear; the entire hit cap is ~420

    As before we tabulate how much threat each option adds, divided by how much threat a point of attack power adds, so the numbers read as attack-power equivalents. And as in the previous table, the third column uses the 10th percentile threat over 10 seconds rather than the average threat over the fight, and each ± is the seed-to-seed standard error over the eight runs. We can see sappers, mangling, and hit all help the bad pulls more than the overall fight, but full party buffs are consistent across the fight and help more than each of those swaps. Sappers come out at 5 ± 1 over the fight average, so spread across three minutes they really do add almost nothing.

    Next, we return to our fury warrior. As before, we do a two-player sim: a P2 best-in-slot fury warrior with Blessing of Salvation and in a group with a feral druid, an enhancement shaman, and two beast-mastery hunters, attacking the same boss as the feral tank. As before, we count the proportion of pulls in which the fury pulls aggro. The two panels show one configuration each, over the same three thousand seeds, with one change between them (a sapper fired at 1.5 seconds). The no-sapper panel sits at 22.6% rather than the 20.5% quoted so far, because the 20.5% baseline already fires its sappers, on the sim's autocast schedule a few seconds in. We see the sapper adds enough threat to the tank that the fury's share drops visibly in the first seconds.

    Here we sim the sapper on the second global cooldown (keeping the opening mangle as the first). On the second global the sapper takes the tank from losing threat in 22.6% of pulls to 12.4%. Left on autocast the sim waits for a global the rotation can spare, which was three seconds in most of the pulls sampled, and it only reaches 20.5%, because half of the losses have already happened by 2.4 seconds. Using the sapper at 1.5 seconds only when the opening mangle fails reaches 18.7%, so it keeps some of the protection while spending a sapper on about one pull in five.
